_note: ACCESSIBILITY as contract, the `<canvas>` verdict shape applied to an animation (canvas/a11y.json — same six fields, same three-surface fold). A Rive artboard is OPAQUE: there is no view tree, only a rendered scene, so the semantics are declared or they do not exist. THE LAW. (1) An animation that conveys meaning takes `a11yLabel` and is an `image`; a decorative one declares nothing and is HIDDEN, which is the right default for a flourish and the reason the error can afford to be an error where it applies. (2) A gesture handler (the same ten words `<canvas>` uses) with neither `a11yLabel` nor `a11yChildren` is a LINT ERROR, code `rive-a11y-label`, failing lint_dsx.rb --strict. (3) `on:stateChange` and `on:event` are REPORTING, not interaction — an animation that tells the app what it did is not a control, and tripping on those would make every instrumented animation an error and teach authors to silence the rule. (4) THE ONE DIVERGENCE FROM CANVAS, and it is Rive's alone: a state machine can carry its OWN pointer listeners inside the .riv file. That makes the component interactive at RUNTIME, so the verdict says so (`interactive`, and a `group` role rather than a hidden node), but it emits NO lint — the linter reads markup, and markup cannot see inside an asset. Two verdicts, one fold, and the difference is stated rather than fudged. (5) `a11yChildren` declares a semantic overlay, exactly as on canvas: the animation becomes a group and each child is a real accessibility element. Function: riveA11y(attrs, a11yChildren, listeners) on all three.

a state machine driven by app state is still decorative by default
a labelled animation is an image
